title: The Gurus answer Farid
hookLine: Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan added their own saloks among Farid's, answering him gently

cards: An old book, passed down in a family. In the margin, a grandfather once wrote: life is hard, I've wasted my years. Decades later, a grandchild wrote beside it: not wasted, it isn't too late.

Two people, perhaps strangers, talking across the page. The Guru Granth Sahib has pages like that. Beside Farid's saloks sit a few short verses marked with the Gurus' names, and read together, they turn out to be replies.

teach.b: Among Sheikh Farid's saloks, the Guru Granth Sahib sets a handful by the Gurus: Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan. Each is marked with its Mahala, so you always know who's speaking.
Some pick up Farid's exact words and turn them, gently. Here are two, in paraphrase.

teach.h: FARID: TOO LATE, HAIR TURNED WHITE.
teach.b: Farid says: those who didn't love the Lord when their hair was black, hardly anyone manages it once the hair turns white. So love the Lord, and your color will be ever new.

teach.h: AMAR DAS: NEVER TOO LATE — GRACE.
teach.b: It sounds like a warning: you may already be too late. Guru Amar Das answers, starting with Farid's own name: Farid, black hair or white, the Lord is always there, if anyone remembers.
And love like that isn't won by effort alone, however much we long; it comes as a gift, by grace. Not too late: the Lord is there at every age.
Elsewhere Farid, in his longing, says: my body burns like an oven, my bones burn like firewood; if my feet grow tired, I'll walk on my head to meet my Beloved.
Guru Nanak answers: don't heat your body like an oven, don't burn your bones. What have your head and feet done wrong?
See your Beloved within. Listen to the tone. The Gurus don't mock Farid or correct him coldly.
They honor his longing, then open a softer door.
That's how the book is built: not one voice lecturing, but a conversation across centuries, held with respect.

how: In the Guru Granth Sahib, each salok is marked with its author, so readers of Farid's saloks can see where Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan reply, and Sikh commentaries read them as a dialogue.

games.q: Farid says: if my feet tire, I'll walk on my head to meet my Beloved. how does Guru Nanak answer?
o: don't burn your body; what have your head and feet done? see your Beloved within.
say Farid is wrong to long for God.
games.why: Guru Nanak honors the longing and turns it inward: the Beloved is found within, not by punishing the body.

practice: Think of someone older than you, a parent, a grandparent, an old teacher, a neighbor, and something they often say that you see differently.
Picture answering them the way the Gurus answered Farid: first honoring what's true in it, then offering your view softly, by name, with respect.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: mahala, the mark that shows which Guru is speaking; it tells you where the replies to Farid begin.

carryVoice: Your line: a conversation across centuries. Even a disagreement can begin with honor. That's day two hundred sixty-two.
